title_eng: Large language models for interpretation of health checkup results

Large language models for interpretation
of health checkup results
Check for updates
Jiwon You 1 & Hangsik Shin 1,2
Large language models (LLMs) show strong generalization, yet their ability to interpret structured
medical data remains insufﬁciently studied. This work evaluated four LLMs— Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini
2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and LLaMA 3.1-70B — using comprehensive health checkup data from the Korean
National Health Insurance Service. Multiple prompting strategies (few-shot, role-based, constraint-
based, and Chain-of-Thought) were tested. Zero-shot accuracy averaged 0.69 (SD 0.06), increasing to
0.92 (0.06) with combined strategies and to 0.95 (0.07) with Chain-of-Thought. Claude Sonnet 4,
Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-4o achieved the highest accuracies ( ≥ 0.98), while LLaMA 3.1-70B showed
lower but improvable performance. Item-level analysis of 10,000 cases demonstrated near-perfect
accuracy (0.99–1.00) for most biochemical markers, including glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, and
liver enzymes. In contrast, blood pressure showed lower accuracy (0.61 –0.91), with age-related
decline, likely due to the complexity of multi-categorical thresholds requiring integration of systolic and
diastolic values. Subgroup analyses revealed model-speci ﬁc biases: sex-related biases were
observed in body mass index (Claude Sonnet 4) and urine protein, serum creatinine, and gamma-
glutamyl transferase (LLaMA 3.1-70B), while age-related biases were identi ﬁed in blood pressure
(Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and hemoglobin (LLaMA
3.1-70B). Overall, advanced prompting markedly improved model performance, and top-tier LLMs
demonstrated robust interpretive capability, while caution is needed for variables with complex clinical
semantics such as blood pressure.

Recent advancements in artiﬁcial intelligence have focused on the use of
large language models (LLMs) across various domains, including health-
care, where their potential as data in terpretation tools is actively being
explored1–5. LLMs are trained on large-scale corpora, such as PubMed
Central, MIMIC-III, CORD-19, and Wikipedia6,7, enabling them to learn
medical terminology and contextual patterns and facilitate tasks such as
summarization and record analysis in addition to providing clinical decision
support. Research validating the p erformance of LLMs across various
medical domains is actively underway, with some studies demonstrating
expert-level capabilities in speciﬁc applications. Notably, GPT-4 (OpenAI,
CA, USA) passed the United States Medical Licensing Examination
(USMLE)8,9, whereas Med-PaLM 2 (Google, CA, USA), which was ﬁne-
tuned on medical data, achieved an accuracy of up to 86.5% on the MedQA
dataset, demonstrating performances approaching those of medical experts,
both specialists and generalist physicians10. GPT-4 demonstrated a perfor-
mance (69%) comparable to that of expert ophthalmologists (median 76%,
range 64–90%), exceeding that of ophthalmo logy trainees (median 59%,
range 57–63%), and markedly outperformingunspecialized junior doctors
(median 43%, range 41–44%)11.
In studies assessing the feasibility ofLLMs as clinical decision-support
tools, GPT-4 demonstrated comparable or superior performance (F1-score
≥ 85%) to that of traditional machine learning-based disease classiﬁcation
models12. However, its performance varied depending on the data format
and complexity. When applied to the American College of Gastroenterology
board exam questions, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic, CA, USA) achieved a
maximum accuracy of 74.0% for text- based questions, whereas the per-
formance for image-based questions decreased by up to 11.4% 13.T h e s e
ﬁndings highlight the potential of LLMsin medical data interpretation while
acknowledging performance variability depending on the data type and
reasoning requirements.
LLMs have greater potential for clini cal interpretation in relatively
simple tasks with large case volumes o r those requiring frequent patient
interactions regarding results. Interpretation of health checkup results
involving standardized measurements such as blood pressure (BP),

cholesterol levels, and other key health indicators requires both accuracy
and context-sensitive reasoning. This straightforward process can harness
the repetitive, large-scale processing capabilities of LLMs. Health checkups
on a national scale generate enormous data, necessitating efﬁcient, repetitive
processing.
According to the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South
Korea, approximately 22 million individuals are eligible for health checkups
annually, with over 75% undergoing examination 14. Although current
health checkup reportsﬂag abnormal values and provide basic interpreta-
tions, patients continue to face signi ﬁcant challenges in interpreting
laboratory test results. More than 60% of patients had difﬁculty in imme-
diately understanding their health checkup results and attempted to inter-
pret them through internet searc hes and similar sources, whereas
approximately 10–17% directly contacted healthcare providers or scheduled
a medical appointment 15. LLMs have the potential to assist patients in
interpreting medical data by generating patient-friendly explanations and
contextual guidance that rule-based systems cannot provide. This capability
positions LLMs as complementary tools that may enhance patient under-
standing and expand the accessibilityto comprehensive health information.
This study examined the utility of LLMs in medical evaluations, spe-
ciﬁcally focusing on the interpretation by class of health checkup results by
using large-scale health checkup data from the NHIS. Speci ﬁcally, we
evaluated four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and
LLaMA 3.1-70B), without priorﬁne-tuning on specialized medical datasets,
to assess their classiﬁcation and diagnostic performance on health checkup
results. Input prompts were designedto simulate real-world health checkup
queries. This study further examined the variability across these models, the
effect of prompt design, and the repro ducibility of the r esults, providing
insights into the performance of different models in health checkup result
classiﬁcation. The overall workﬂow of the study is illustrated in Fig.1.
Results
Effect of Prompt Type and Few-Shot Examples on Model
Performance
Table 1 illustrates the performance variation in the classi ﬁcation of
health checkup results across diffe rent prompting strategies. Upon
analyzing the performance variatio ns across different prompt types,
the combination prompting strategy based on role-based, few-shot,
constraints and Chain-of-Though t (CoT) emerged as the highest-
performing method across all LLMs. A comparative evaluation of the
performance variability induced by the few-shot examples in the
combined prompting revealed performance discrepancies for certain
health checkup items; however, no statistically signi ﬁcant differences
were observed in the average performance across all items. Based on

Performance of LLMs in Interpreting Health Checkup Results
We evaluated the accuracy and reproducibility of the classi ﬁcation of
health checkup results across the LLMs, revealing notable differences in
performance for individual examination items. Table 2 presents the
classiﬁcation accuracy for each model, including the mean accuracy values
and standard deviations (SD). The radar charts in Fig. 2A, B present a
visual comparison of the model performance across the health checkup
items. Among the four models, Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Pro
achieved the highest accuracy of 0.99, followed closely by GPT-4o with
0.98. LLaMA 3.1-70B yielded the lowest mean accuracy at 0.84, which was
signiﬁcantly lower than that of the other models (p < 0.001). All reported
values represent the average of three independent runs under identical
conditions to ensure reproducibility.
Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Pro demonstrated the highest overall
performance with minimal variability (SD < 0.01). It consistently achieved
near-perfect classiﬁcation across most items, including a perfect accuracy of
1.00 for fasting blood glucose (FBG), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides
(TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDLC), aspartate amino-
transferase (AST), urine protein (UP),and alanine aminotransferase (ALT),
and very high accuracy for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLC;
0.99), hemoglobin (Hb; 0.98), and body mass index (BMI; > 0.97). Even in
the more challenging analysis of the BP results, Claude Sonnet 4 (0.91)
outperformed the other models outperformed the other models, followed
closely by Gemini 2.5 Pro at 0.89. GPT-4o attained a mean accuracy of 0.98.
It attained a perfect accuracy (1.00) for FBG, TC, TG, HDLC, UP, AST, and
ALT, and maintained a strong performance for LDLC (0.98) and serum
creatinine (SC; 0.98). Nevertheless, it showed a relatively lower perfor-
mances for BP (0.88), indicating that BP assessment was the most chal-
lenging item for all models. By cont rast, LLaMA 3.1-70B exhibited the
lowest overall performance, with a mean accuracy of 0.85 (SD = 0.01).
Although it performed well for certain items such as SC (0.97), AST (0.98),
and ALT (0.97), it consistently underperformed for BMI (0.59), BP (0.61),
and LDLC (0.66). Across all models, FBG, TC, TG, HDLC, SC, AST, ALT,
and UP were classiﬁed with very high accuracies (0.97–1.00), demonstrating
the relative simplicity of these classiﬁcation tasks. By contrast, BP emerged
as the most challenging item to assess for all models, with marked perfor-
mance gaps between Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 pro, GPT-4o (0.88–0.91),
and LLaMA 3.1-70B (0.61). Similarly, the assessments of TC, LDLC, Hb and
gamma-glutamyl transferase ( γ-GTP) revealed disparities, with Claude
Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-4o consistently achieving accuracies of
> 0.95 whereas LLaMA lagged behind (< 0.88). Figure2C presents the mean
accuracy across all tasks for the four evaluated models.
Statistical comparisons using a bi nomial generalized linear model
(GLM) and Cohen’s h revealed practical performance differences between
the models for BMI, BP, FBG, TC, HDLC, LDLC, Hb, and γ-GTP. By
contrast, no signiﬁcant differences were observed for TG, UP, SC, AST, or
ALT (Supplementary Table 9). Post- hoc pairwise proportion tests with
Holm correction demonstrated no signiﬁcant differences in performance
